lessons.title: Case Study: 1.5 Crore Rupees in Hyderabad, a 3BHK Flat vs a Pre-Leased Office Unit

children.text: Anil and Kavya, both 38, work at technology companies in Hyderabad and already own the flat they live in. After an ESOP sale and years of saving, they have ₹1.5 crore to invest in property for the next 10 years. Both are in the 30% tax bracket. Their friends are split. Half say "buy a flat in the western corridor, Hyderabad prices only go up". The other half say "buy a pre-leased office, why settle for 3% rent?" This case study runs both options the way a professional investor would: due diligence, year-one cash flow, a 10-year after-tax model with good and bad scenarios, and a decision.

body.text: The right property is not the one with the best brochure number. It is the one whose realistic bad case you can live with, measured after costs, tax and time.

body.caption: Option A vs Option B, ₹1.5 crore deployed in each

cells: Stamp duty, registration and other costs
₹75 per sq ft, ₹97,500 a month (₹11.7 lakh a year)
9-year lease in its third year; lock-in ends in 12 months; 15% escalation every 3 years

columns.label: Option A: the flat
points: RERA-registered project with occupancy certificate
Rents in the society range from ₹36,000 to ₹40,000
More than 40 flats in the same society listed for sale, signalling plenty of competition on resale
Society maintenance of about ₹7,400 a month, paid by the owner
Price growth in the corridor has been strong, but depends on continued IT hiring and infrastructure

columns.label: Option B: the office
points: Lease deed verified; rent confirmed in the seller's bank statements and Form 26AS
Tenant is profitable and listed, but its lock-in ends in 12 months
Passing rent of ₹75 is at the upper end of the ₹70 to ₹78 range for similar strata space
Building is 8 years old, with about 60 owners and no green certification
New Grade A supply in the Financial District could pull tenants away over time

body.text: Notice that the GST question never arises for Option B. Annual rent of ₹11.7 lakh is below the ₹20 lakh registration threshold, so Anil and Kavya stay unregistered, and their GST-registered tenant pays GST on the rent under reverse charge.

children.text: Year One: What Lands in Their Account

stats.label: Option A: year 1 cash after costs and tax
Option B: year 1 cash after costs and tax

children.text: For the flat, ₹4.56 lakh of rent minus 30% for maintenance, property tax, vacancy and repairs leaves ₹3.19 lakh, and income tax takes ₹93,000 more. For the office, ₹11.7 lakh of rent minus ₹40,000 of property tax and insurance leaves ₹11.3 lakh. Tax on house property income of (₹11.7 lakh minus ₹30,000 property tax) × 70% × 30% is ₹2.39 lakh, leaving ₹8.91 lakh. Year one is not close. But property returns are decided over the full holding period, and especially at exit.
Each option is modelled under three scenarios, without a loan, after income tax on rent and 12.5% capital gains tax on sale.

Flat: rent grows 5% a year; 30% of gross rent goes to running costs and vacancy; property tax of ₹15,000 is deducted before the 30% standard deduction; price grows at 4%, 7% or 9% a year; 1% brokerage on sale.

Office upside and base: rent steps up 15% in years 2 and 5; the lease expires after year 7 and the tenant renews at the same rent, with one month's brokerage; the new lease's first 15% escalation falls in year 11, which the buyer prices in. Exit at a cap rate of 7.75% (upside) or 8.5% (base) on year 11 net income of ₹17.39 lakh.

Office downside: the tenant leaves when its lock-in ends after year 1. The unit sits empty for 9 months, with the owner paying CAM of ₹13,000 a month, then re-leases at ₹68 per sq ft with 3 rent-free months and 2 months' brokerage. Rent then steps up 15% every 3 years. Exit at a 9.5% cap rate, reflecting an older building.

Both: ₹1.5 crore invested at the start; stamp duty is added to the cost when computing capital gains; tax at 30% on house property income; surcharge, cess and the tenant's security deposit are ignored.

body.caption: Year 11 rent minus owner costs, divided by the exit cap rate, before 1% brokerage and capital gains tax.
10-year results, all figures after costs and tax

children.text: In the base cases, the office returns 9.2% after tax against 7.0% for the flat. For the flat to match the office's base case, Tellapur prices would need to rise about 9.5% a year for ten years. Both options have a bad case that lands in roughly the same place, around 4.5%, but they get there for completely different reasons.

events.title: Full rent, then the lock-in ends
events.description: The tenant consolidates into a new Grade A campus in the Financial District and gives notice.

events.title: No rent at all
events.description: Nine months vacant and three rent-free months for the new tenant, plus ₹2.94 lakh of CAM and brokerage.

events.title: New tenant at ₹68 per sq ft
events.description: Rent restarts at ₹10.6 lakh a year, about 9% below the previous tenant's starting rent.

events.title: Escalations resume
events.description: Rent climbs to ₹14 lakh a year by year 9, below where the original lease would have been.

events.title: Sale at a 9.5% cap rate
events.description: An older strata building sells for ₹1.43 crore, below the ₹1.5 crore invested, producing a capital loss.

body.text: The office's outcome hinges on one event: whether a single tenant stays past a lock-in that ends in 12 months. That one decision swings the after-tax IRR from about 9.2% to about 4.7%. The flat has no single make-or-break moment, but its outcome hinges entirely on a price trend nobody controls.

Look at the flat at 9% growth. It returns a higher money multiple (2.23x) than the office base case (2.04x), yet a lower IRR (8.8% vs 9.2%). The flat pays almost everything at the very end, while the office pays steadily along the way. Cash received earlier is worth more.

body.title: What each option is really a bet on

columns.label: Option A is a bet that
points: Western Hyderabad prices keep rising strongly for 10 years
Oversupply in the society does not cap resale prices
The family end-user market stays deep when they sell
They are happy with very little cash income in the meantime

columns.label: Option B is a bet that
points: This tenant, or an equally good one, keeps the unit occupied
An ageing strata building holds its appeal against new Grade A supply
Cap rates do not rise sharply by the time they sell
They can handle a year with no rent if the tenant leaves

children.text: They chose Option B, but not on the seller's terms. The biggest risk was the lock-in ending in 12 months, so they made their offer conditional on the tenant signing a lease amendment with a fresh three-year lock-in, and asked the seller to share the cost of a small rent concession to secure it. They also agreed to keep ₹12 lakh, about a year's rent, in a liquid fund as a vacancy reserve. If the tenant had refused, their plan B was to split the money between listed REITs and a smaller residential purchase rather than take the downside risk undiversified.

body.title: Calculate: Year 1 After-Tax Yield on the Office
body.prompt: Option B earns ₹11.7 lakh of rent in year 1. The owner pays ₹40,000 of property tax and insurance. Income tax is 30% of (rent minus ₹30,000 property tax) × 70%. What is the year 1 after-tax cash as a percentage of the ₹1.5 crore invested? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Net before tax: ₹11.7 lakh minus ₹0.4 lakh = ₹11.3 lakh. Tax: (₹11.7 lakh minus ₹0.3 lakh) × 0.7 × 0.3 = ₹2.394 lakh. After tax: ₹8.906 lakh. As a share of ₹150 lakh: 5.94%.

body.title: Quick Check: Multiple vs IRR
body.question: The flat at 9% growth returns 2.23x money but an 8.8% IRR, while the office base case returns 2.04x but a 9.2% IRR. Why?
options: The IRR calculation ignores the sale price
The office pays much more of its return as rent in the early years, and IRR rewards earlier cash
The flat pays more income tax on rent
Money multiples include inflation and IRR does not
body.explanation: The flat delivers most of its cash in year 10 through the sale, while the office delivers over ₹1 crore of after-tax rent along the way. IRR accounts for timing, so steady earlier cash scores higher even with a smaller total.

body.title: Scenario: Same Choice, Different Investor
body.scenario: Mrs. Reddy, 66, a retired school principal in Hyderabad, also has ₹1.5 crore from selling her late husband's ancestral land. Her pension covers about half her monthly expenses, and she wants the rest from this money. She has no other investments and dislikes dealing with brokers and paperwork. Her nephew shows her the same two options.
body.prompt: Should she choose A, B, or neither? Explain using the case study results.
body.modelAnswer: Neither in its current form. Option A pays her only about ₹2.3 lakh a year after costs and tax, around ₹19,000 a month, far too little to cover half her expenses, and its return depends on selling at a high price years later. Option B pays about ₹8.9 lakh a year, which fits her income need much better, but its downside case includes a full year with no rent, exactly when she could least afford it. And with no other assets, all ₹1.5 crore would ride on one tenant. Managing a lease, TDS records and a possible re-leasing search also does not suit her. A better route would be a diversified mix: listed REITs for commercial rental income with daily liquidity, plus conventional fixed-income options suited to a retiree, discussed with a SEBI-registered investment adviser. If she insists on direct property, Option B only makes sense with a long fresh lock-in and a vacancy reserve set aside first.

body.title: Run Your Own Case Study
steps: Write down your horizon, tax bracket and how much cash income you need each year
Verify rent, lease terms and tenant quality for every option
Calculate year 1 cash after all costs and tax
Model at least three scenarios over your full horizon, including a realistic bad case
Compare after-tax IRR, not just yield or appreciation
Identify the single event that most changes each outcome
Decide which bad case you could actually live through, and plan a cash reserve for it

points: On ₹1.5 crore in Hyderabad, the pre-leased office paid ₹8.91 lakh after tax in year 1 against ₹2.27 lakh for the flat.
Over 10 years, the base cases returned about 9.2% after tax for the office and 7.0% for the flat.
The flat needed about 9.5% annual price growth to match the office's base case.
Both options had bad cases near 4.5% to 4.7%, one driven by a tenant leaving, the other by weak price growth.
IRR rewards the office's steady rent; the flat can win on money multiple yet lose on IRR because its return comes at the end.
The smartest move was to reduce the biggest identified risk before buying, by securing a fresh lock-in and a vacancy reserve.

body.text: This case study uses fictional investors, illustrative prices, rents and assumptions, and a simplified tax treatment that ignores surcharge, cess and security deposits. It is not a forecast for Hyderabad property or any specific building. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy any property or investment.
